title: Why tellers matter
hook: a story lives because someone tells it well and truly

segments.voice: Yesterday, a pauri: one stanza, read for its picture, its twist and its point. Your line was one picture, one point.

A grandmother at the end of a family dinner, telling how she came to this country. The grandkids have heard it before. One of them corrects a detail; she waves it off and keeps going. Years later she's gone, and that grandkid is the one at the end of the table, telling it to the next lot. Some details are different now. Is it still her story? Whether a story survives depends less on the story than on the people who keep telling it. Today: katha.
screen: `A STORY AT THE END OF DINNER.` → `THE GRANDKID TELLS IT NEXT.` → `IS IT STILL HER STORY?`

segments.voice: Sikhs have a word for the spoken telling and explaining of Gurbani in the gurdwara: katha. A katha teacher sits before the sangat, takes a line, and opens it up with stories and pictures. Bhai Gurdas did a version of that in verse, carrying the Guru's teaching in the language of the fields and the bazaar, so people could hold on to it. Bhai Nand Lal did it in Persian, for listeners who loved that kind of poetry. That's why this block has called them tellers. Two words carry today's lesson: well and truly. They pull in different directions, and a good teller holds both. Well means the story has to land; if nobody can follow it, it dies with the teller. Yesterday's sandalwood and bamboo is told well. Truly means the teller doesn't bend the story to look good, or to win an argument. And telling well can tempt you away from telling truly: a detail gets bigger with each retelling because it gets a better reaction. That's why, starting next week, this path reads the janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak, carefully. Different tellers told them differently, and the Sikhs who kept them have had to think about which tellings to trust. One more thing. Every Sikh who explains the Guru's teaching to a child at a kitchen table is a teller too. The chain didn't stop with Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal. It runs through any household that passes the stories on.
screen: `KATHA: THE TELLING IN THE GURDWARA.` · `WELL: THE STORY HAS TO LAND.` · `TRULY: DON'T BEND IT.` · `EVERY HOUSEHOLD IS A TELLER.` · then, large: `TELL IT TRUE.`

segments.voice: Choose a story you've told more than once, from your family, your work, your own life, and run it through the way you usually tell it. Then run it again and listen for the places where it's grown, the bit made a little funnier, a little bigger, a little kinder to yourself, and just notice where the true version is. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end.
Katha, the spoken telling and explaining of Gurbani in the gurdwara, kept alive and true the way Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal told it.
Your line: tell it true. Told well to live, told truly to stay itself. That's seven hundred twenty days.

chat.meaning: Katha is the spoken telling and explaining of Gurbani. A good teller tells it well, so it lands, and truly, without bending it.
